questions: why does the map seem to stop on July 27 if the Madrid fire lasted fourteen days?
Are there local detections after July 27, and is fourteen days verified?

request.user_question: why does the map seem to stop on July 27 if the Madrid fire lasted fourteen days?

conversation.content: why does the map seem to stop on July 27 if the Madrid fire lasted fourteen days?

The satellite map appears to stop because orbital sensors capture active thermal emissions rather than administrative wildfire milestones [K10] [5]. In the Sierra Oeste, local satellite observations peaked and then declined sharply, leaving only sparse residual thermal detections through early August [5]. A drop in detections reflects heat output falling below sensor detection limits rather than official containment or extinction [K10] [5]. 

Observations consistent with active burning do not constitute administrative confirmation of an incident's total duration [K10] [5]. Official regional reports confirm major wildfire activity in the area [W1] [W3], but the user's claimed fourteen-day duration is not verified by official records [W1] [W3]. Ground response, mop-up operations, and post-fire monitoring typically continue for many days after open flaming and intense heat cease to trigger spaceborne sensors [K10] [5].
Are there local detections after July 27, and is fourteen days verified?

Local satellite detections do exist after July 27 [5]. Following the peak activity, the sensor timeline records 70 detections on July 28, 2 on July 30, 5 on July 31, 14 on August 1, and isolated single detections on August 7 and August 9 [5]. While thermal detections are satellite observations rather than confirmed fire perimeters, these data demonstrate that local heat anomalies continued past late July [K2] [5]. 

The claimed fourteen-day duration is not verified from the available evidence. While incident reports confirm that the Sierra Oeste fires remained active with slowing progression by July 28 [W5], verified administrative records declaring official containment or final extinction dates are missing. Confirming a specific fourteen-day operational duration requires retrieved official containment declarations from emergency management agencies rather than satellite observation cutoffs alone [K2] [W5].

result.title: Thermal episode duration
result.text: The episode profiling tool discovers the greatest daily energy within available history when no date is specified. It computes consecutive above-background activity in a window of 15 days before and after the peak, with robust same-month background from other years. This is a statistical thermal episode that can include several fires. It is not the official ignition, containment or extinction interval. result.title: Fire radiative power and energy
result.text: FRP is instantaneous fire radiative power in MW, equivalent to MJ per second. FRE is energy integrated over time in MJ. One GJ is 1000 MJ. Summing instantaneous satellite FRP samples does not give energy. The local scientific energy tool integrates calibrated daily FRE over the cube cells represented each day. Estimates depend on temporal reconstruction and sensor coverage.

result.title: Reconstruction and uncertainty
result.text: RTS Kalman smoothing estimates missing daily thermal measurements using a state model, other available sensors and a historical cross-sensor prior. A reconstructed value is an estimate, not a direct observation or proof of a continuing fire. A 95 percent model interval describes uncertainty of the modeled state; it is not the probability that a named fire occurred. Partially reconstructed days can also contain real observations.

Asimismo, anunció que la Comunidad de Madrid ya trabaja en la puesta en marcha de una línea específica de ayudas, a través del Plan de Inversión Regional, para apoyar a los ayuntamientos y municipios afectados. id='[W101]' source_type='WEB_NEWS_REPORT' title='Madrid emergency coordination report on merged Sierra Oeste fire fronts' authors_or_agency='Comunidad de Madrid' year=2026 dataset_or_doi='Official report; article text retrieved; incident match unconfirmed' url='https://www.comunidad.madrid/noticias/2026/07/25/diaz-ayuso-todos-medios-region-estan-trabajando-descanso' relevance_note='Retrieved article text (location/date match must still be checked):
La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha advertido de la gravedad del gran incendio que afecta a la Sierra Oeste tras participar en la reunión del Centro de Coordinación Operativa (CECOP) celebrada en el Puesto de Mando Avanzado (PMA) instalado en Cenicientos.
Díaz Ayuso ha explicado que la situación está cambiando "a gran velocidad" y que el incendio atraviesa "un momento muy crítico". Según señaló, los distintos focos han generado "una especie de propia atmósfera" y ya "se comportan como uno solo", una situación que calificó como "totalmente inédita, nunca vista", lo que lleva a las autoridades a temer "situaciones mucho peores".
La presidenta indicó que se está evacuando a todas las poblaciones del Valle del Tiétar y ha advertido de que el incendio también afectará a esta parte de la Comunidad de Madrid. Asimismo, subrayó que "todos los medios de la región están trabajando sin descanso" para hacer frente a la emergencia y pidió a la población que no se acerque a la zona para facilitar el trabajo de los servicios de emergencia y mantener despejadas las vías de acceso. También agradeció la comprensión y la paciencia de los ciudadanos, asegurando que esa colaboración está siendo clave para afrontar la situación.
En el ámbito sanitario, Díaz Ayuso anunció un refuerzo extraordinario del sistema regional con otras 800 camas, que podrán dar servicio a los municipios de la provincia de Ávila si fuera necesario. Además, informó de la activación de otras 241 camas, con 12 puestos de UCI, en el Hospital público Enfermera Isabel Zendal, que permanecerán a disposición de las distintas necesidades que puedan surgir como consecuencia de la emergencia.
La presidenta también avanzó una medida para facilitar los trámites administrativos a los vecinos de las zonas afectadas. En este sentido, anunció que el Servicio Regional de Empleo renovará automáticamente todas las demandas de empleo de los habitantes de los municipios afectados por los incendios, con el objetivo de evitar desplazamientos innecesarios mientras se mantenga la situación de emergencia.'

id='[W102]' source_type='WEB_NEWS_REPORT' title='Madrid report on operational de-escalation and continuing evacuations' authors_or_agency='Comunidad de Madrid' year=2026 dataset_or_doi='Official report; article text retrieved; incident match unconfirmed' url='https://www.comunidad.madrid/noticias/2026/07/30/diaz-ayuso-comprueba-situacion-terreno-afectado-incendios-sierra-oeste' relevance_note='Retrieved article text (location/date match must still be checked):
La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha comprobado la situación del terreno afectado por los incendios de la Sierra Oeste desde el helicóptero de coordinación y vigilancia de la Agencia de Seguridad y Emergencias 112 de la Comunidad de Madrid (ASEM112).
Acompañada del director de la Agencia, Pedro Ruiz, han llevado a cabo un reconocimiento de la zona, con el fin de conocer de primera mano su estado y ajustar las actuaciones de reconstrucción. La estimación inicial apunta a más de 27.000 hectáreas afectadas tras una semana con el fuego.
Este jueves el incendio se ha rebajado a Situación Operativa 2, aunque permanecen evacuadas las urbanizaciones de San Martín de Valdeiglesias y Pelayos de la presa, las más cercanas al pantano de San Juan.
La Comunidad de Madrid ha acordado un conjunto de actuaciones por valor de cerca de 100 millones de euros para la reconstrucción de la zona, con medidas para facilitar el acceso a la vivienda, apoyo, psicosocial, ayudas para autónomos, comerciantes, agricultores y ganadero, así como planes para recuperar el patrimonio natural.'

result.title: Satellite detections and incident identity
result.text: NASA FIRMS detections are satellite thermal anomalies, not a count of distinct fires. A single fire may generate many detections over different sensors and days. The application uses calibrated FRE rather than raw counts for scientific energy comparisons.

id='[W2]' source_type='WEB_NEWS_REPORT' title='elpais.com' authors_or_agency='english.elpais.com' year=2026 dataset_or_doi='News report; article text retrieved; incident match unconfirmed' url='https://english.elpais.com/spain/2026-07-28/race-against-time-in-spains-wildfire-battle-24-critical-hours-before-the-heatwave.html' relevance_note='Retrieved article text (location/date match must still be checked):
Beatriz OlaizolaMadrid - Jul 28, 2026 - 07:44CESTShare on WhatsappShare on FacebookShare on TwitterDesplegar Redes SocialesPrefer EL PAÍS on GoogleCompartir:WhatsappFacebookTwitterBlueskyLinkedinCopy linkThe wildfires ravaging the Spanish province of Ávila in the Castilla y León region and the Madrid region remain active, although their advance has slowed. Firefighting operations continue to be extremely challenging, hampered by strong and shifting winds. After several days of rapid spread, crews managed on Sunday to bring many of the fire fronts under control. However, a number of the most active areas of the blazes remain burning, and the fires are still far from being fully contained. Efforts are focused on stabilizing these critical fronts, while also protecting nearby communities and preventing the two major fire zones, which are drawing ever closer together, from merging. Emergency crews are carrying out a coordinated assault on the areas burning most intensely.“Today and tomorrow are absolutely crucial days, because from Wednesday onward the weather forecasts are really negative from the point of view of fighting the fire,” said Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, referring to the fact that a fourth heat wave is expected to last until Sunday.“We have to stay positive; we have control of the emergency. We do have to acknowledge that we are moving slowly because the weather conditions are not helping us at all,” he added from the command post in Navalcarnero, near MadridFrom there, Madrid regional premier Isabel Díaz Ayuso summed up the situation in a single word: “Hellish.”Firefighters and authorities agree that the situation is evolving positively, albeit very slowly, and that the risk of flare-ups remains high, especially with the new heat wave set to reach the Iberian Peninsula on Wednesday. Spain’s Military Emergency Unit (UME) is managing the incidents as a single wildfire, and the government has extended the national emergency declaration to Toledo, in the Castilla-La Mancha region, where in nine of the 11 evacuated municipalities have been authorized to return.Across the three regions (Madrid, Castilla-La Mancha and Castilla y León), 77,000 hectares have already been affected, and 90,149 people have been evacuated or confined, a figure expected to decrease once the number of resettled residents is updated. In Ávila alone, 50,000 hectares have burned, making it the largest and “most aggressive” wildfire in Spain’s history. In total, the fires encompass a perimeter of 280 kilometers (174 miles), according to Civil Protection data.To understand the scale of the disaster, two figures stand out: Ávila has a total surface area of about 804,872 hectares, meaning the burned area represents 6.21% of the province; and in Madrid, which covers 802,800 hectares, 3.11% of the region is being consumed by the flames.At night, firefighters take advantage of lower temperatures and increased humidity to try to stabilize the fires and gradually tackle the most worrying hotspots, such as the San Juan Reservoir area in Madrid and the fires in Mijares and Casillas in Ávila. Once again, all eyes are on the weather, and there is a sense of cautious optimism. According to Spain’s interior minister, “the weather forecast will not be as favorable as they would like.” Even so, there are still two days ahead during which crews “can be proactive,” Grande-Marlaska noted. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez also warned, as he had on Sunday, that “difficult hours still lie ahead” due to the forecast heat wave.In response to the situation, the government has announced that it will approve a legislative decree at Tuesday’s Cabinet meeting to extend protections for workers and businesses affected by wildfires across different parts of the country. This includes an extraordinary benefit that will cover situations not previously contemplated, such as workers who are unable to report to their jobs because they have been evacuated, have lost their homes, or no longer have access to basic services.Conditions facing firefighters in Madrid’s Sierra Oeste, where 25,000 hectares have been affected, and in Ávila are worse than they were on Sunday, though still not as severe as in the previous days. “They are not yet as bad as when the fire first broke out,” Javier Armenteros, the representative for Spain’s state meteorological agency AEMET in the Madrid region, told EL PAÍS. “But conditions are gradually deteriorating,” he added. Temperatures are a particular concern: Monday will be the last day with highs below 35ºC (95ºF), while temperatures are expected to rise to 38ºC (100ºF) from Tuesday. Another key factor is relative humidity. The air will be “drier than it was over the weekend,” dropping below 20% during the hottest part of the day.The battle at the San Juan reservoirIn the Madrid region, three areas are causing particular concern: the surroundings of the Cofio River; the fire fronts near Cadalso de los Vidrios and Villa del Prado; and the residential developments south of the San Juan reservoir, around the town of San Martín de Valdeiglesias. Firefighting efforts are now concentrated in these areas.The eastern flank of the fire has been stabilized, and crews are working to steadily cool burned terrain and prevent flare-ups. On the western side, closer to Ávila, however, the blaze is still “putting up a fight,” according to the central government’s representative in the region, Francisco Martín.“The situation remains extremely complex,” said Martin. “Our priority at the moment is the area around the San Juan reservoir. An extraordinary deployment is working intensively to contain that front and prevent it from reaching the town of Valdemaqueda [population 870].”There are now 13 evacuated municipalities and three under lockdown in the Madrid region. In total, 31,865 people are spending the night away from their homes, while a further 19,262 remain confined to their towns and villages.There has, however, been some positive news: the 4,500 people evacuated from the El Escorial campsite have been allowed to return, and elderly residents who were moved from a care home in San Martín de Valdeiglesias have also been able to go back to the facility.🌙 Otra noche de intenso trabajo.Seguimos trabajando sin descanso para combatir los grandes incendios de esta #EmergenciaNacional 🎥 Misiones en Sotillo de la Adrada pic.twitter.com/yZg9DNQUqF— UME (@UMEgob) July 27, 2026


‘We’ve faced moments of great danger’The wildfire in Burgohondo, in the province of Ávila, also remains out of control, although its rate of spread has slowed. The nights have been far from easy, with strong gusts of wind hampering firefighting efforts and creating tense situations, such as the one in the municipality of Sotillo, where burning embers, carried aloft by the wind, flew across a road that firefighters were trying to defend.Similar scenes have played out in other areas. Particular concern surrounds Casillas (population 673), where some buildings and homes have been damaged, and Mijares (718 inhabitants). The fire is intensifying in certain locations while remaining more or less under control in others. The response has become a highly targeted operation: containing the flames where possible, pulling back when fire activity intensifies, and then moving in again.The blaze, which broke out last Wednesday, has now reached an estimated perimeter of 160 kilometres (99 miles) on both sides of the Sierra de Gredos. “The perimeter is extremely large, as is the burned area,” said Alejandro Peñalvo, the incident commander for the Burgohondo fire.Even so, the situation is “considerably more favorable” than had been feared. Work carried out on Monday by the extensive force deployed against the southern fire has yielded results, according to José Luis Gutiérrez, the chief firefighting officer for Castilla y León’s regional wildfire emergency plan (INFOCAL).“We have faced moments of great danger, particularly while defending the area around the Casillas mountain pass, the entrance to the Iruelas Nature Reserve and the El Tiemblo chestnut forest, as well as the Mijares pass,” he said.The largest wildfire in Spain’s history has forced the evacuation of 25,087 people across 16 municipalities in the region, while a further 8,735 residents in four municipalities have been ordered to remain indoors. These figures come on top of those affected in Toledo, which is also under a national emergency declaration.Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get more English-language news coverage from EL PAÍS USA EditionArchived InMadridFernando Grande-MarlaskaÁvilaToledoIsabel Díaz Ayuso'

citations.title: Satellite detections and incident identity
citations.relevance_note: NASA FIRMS detections are satellite thermal anomalies, not a count of distinct fires. A single fire may generate many detections over different sensors and days. Thermal anomalies can also be agricultural burning or industrial sources. A selected polygon or H3 hexagon is a query area, not a confirmed wildfire perimeter. Zero detections do not prove absence of fire: clouds, overpasses, thresholds and archive coverage affect observation. Thermal sensors can detect flaming and sufficiently hot smoldering. A decline in detection counts alone cannot distinguish less combustion from obscuration, sampling or detection thresholds; none of these is a measured explanation without matching evidence.
